question: What does the inertial sensor system (ISS) at the heart of an INS consist of?

options.text: A radio receiver and a navigation database
A flux valve, a gyro and a heading indicator
Pitot-static sensors, temperature probes and an air data computer
A gyro and accelerometer platform, and a computer

explanation: The inertial sensor system is a stable platform carrying high-quality gyros and accelerometers, together with a computer. Adding a second computer to store waypoints and steer between them turns it into an inertial navigation system.

question: How does the INS computer obtain velocity from the accelerometers?

options.text: By integrating acceleration once with time
By differentiating acceleration with time
By dividing acceleration by the elapsed time squared
By integrating acceleration twice with time

explanation: Integrating acceleration over time gives velocity. Integrating that velocity a second time gives distance travelled, from which position is updated.

question: How does an INS obtain distance travelled?

options.text: By multiplying acceleration by elapsed time
By counting the Schuler oscillations
By integrating velocity with time, the second integration
By integrating acceleration once with time

explanation: The first integration turns acceleration into velocity, the second turns velocity into distance. The distance north and east is then applied to the start position.

question: Which of these can an inertial sensor system provide without any outside reference?

options.text: Indicated airspeed, pressure altitude and Mach number
True heading, drift and ground speed
Radio bearings from ground stations
Magnetic variation, measured directly

explanation: The ISS gives pitch, roll, true heading, true track, drift, present position, ground speed and wind (with a TAS input). Airspeed and pressure altitude come from the air data computer.

question: What turns an inertial sensor system into an inertial navigation system?

options.text: A radio altimeter that limits vertical errors
A computer that stores and steers to waypoints
A flux valve that supplies magnetic heading
A second set of accelerometers on the vertical axis

explanation: The extra navigation computer lets the crew enter and store waypoints and computes track angle error, distance and time to go. These outputs can be used by the autopilot, flight director or for manual flying.

question: What was special about the inertial navigation system when it was introduced?

options.text: It was the first system to show magnetic heading
It was the first system to use ground radio stations
It was the first self-contained source of all of it
It was the first system that needed no electrical power of any kind

explanation: The INS needs no external reference once aligned and gives all the navigation data from one unit. The similar laser-gyro IRS has since joined it.

question: Why must the accelerometers of a gimballed INS be kept horizontal?

options.text: So that the gyros do not precess
So that they can be aligned with magnetic north
So that they measure vertical speed directly
So that they do not sense gravity

explanation: A tilted horizontal accelerometer senses part of gravity's 1 g and treats it as an aircraft acceleration, producing a false velocity. The platform is therefore kept level with the local horizontal.

question: In a north-aligned INS, how are the two horizontal accelerometers arranged?

options.text: One on the north-south axis, one on the east-west axis
One along the longitudinal axis, one vertical
Both along the east-west axis, for redundancy
Both along the aircraft's longitudinal axis

explanation: The north and east accelerometers measure accelerations along true north-south and east-west. Their integrated outputs are the north and east velocities and distances.

question: What holds the INS platform stable in space?

options.text: A magnetic detector unit in the wing tip
The accelerometers acting as torque motors
The weight of the platform hanging below its pivot
Gyros on the platform, driving the gimbal motors

explanation: The platform gyros sense any rotation of the platform and drive torque motors on the gimbals to cancel it, keeping the platform level and aligned.

question: The east-west distance gone from an INS is a departure. How is it turned into change of longitude?

options.text: It is multiplied by the cosine of the latitude
It is multiplied by the sine of the latitude
It is multiplied by the secant of the latitude
It is divided by the secant of the latitude

explanation: Departure = change of longitude × cos latitude, so change of longitude = departure × sec latitude. Meridians converge, so one nautical mile of departure covers more longitude at high latitude.

question: An INS measures 120 NM of easterly departure at a mean latitude of 60°N. What change of longitude is that?

options.text: 60 minutes, that is 1°
240 minutes, that is 4°
208 minutes, about 3.5°
120 minutes, that is 2°

explanation: Change of longitude = departure × sec latitude = 120 × 2 = 240 minutes of longitude, which is 4°. Multiplying by cos 60° instead gives the 60-minute slip.

question: In a north-referenced INS, the second integration of the north-south acceleration gives:

options.text: Change of latitude
Departure, the east-west distance gone
Change of longitude
North-south velocity

explanation: The first integration gives north-south speed; the second gives north-south distance, which is change of latitude in nautical miles (minutes of arc). The east-west channel gives departure.

question: In flight, which effects must the computer of a north-referenced INS compensate for?

options.text: Magnetic variation and deviation
Earth rate, transport rate and Coriolis
Altimeter temperature error only
Instrument, position, density and compressibility error

explanation: To keep the platform level and pointing north the computer allows for earth rate, transport rate (movement over the curved earth) and Coriolis and centripetal accelerations.

question: Why must the stable element of an INS be aligned before use?

options.text: The battery must be charged during alignment
The gyros must be set to magnetic north
The waypoints for the route cannot be loaded until it is aligned
The accelerometers must sense along known axes

explanation: The platform must be aligned in attitude (level) and in azimuth (true north) so that each accelerometer measures acceleration along its chosen axis.

question: What is the first stage of an INS alignment sequence?

options.text: Warm-up of the fluid-filled parts to operating temperature
Fine levelling of the platform, to within 6 seconds of arc
Entering the waypoints for the flight
Gyrocompassing, to find true north

explanation: Alignment starts with a warm-up of the fluid-filled components to their correct temperature, then coarse alignment, fine levelling and gyrocompassing.

question: How long does the INS warm-up phase normally take?

options.text: About 10 seconds
About 84 minutes
About 3 to 4 minutes
About 15 to 20 minutes

explanation: Bringing the fluid-filled components to their operating temperature normally takes 3 to 4 minutes, before the platform can be levelled and aligned.

question: During coarse levelling, what is used as the reference to level the platform roughly?

options.text: The pilot's entry of the aircraft heading
The radio altimeter, the air data computer and the flux valve
The flux valve and the standby compass
The airframe, gravity switches or accelerometers

explanation: Pitch and roll gimbals are first driven to 90° to each other, then the platform is roughly levelled against the airframe or using gravity switches or the horizontal accelerometers.

question: How is coarse azimuth alignment achieved?

options.text: It is turned to the best known true heading
The accelerometer outputs are reduced to zero
The east gyro is connected to the azimuth motor
The platform is aligned with magnetic north from the flux valve

explanation: Coarse azimuth alignment turns the platform until its heading output agrees with the aircraft's best known true heading. Gyrocompassing later refines it.

question: How closely does coarse alignment level and align the platform, and how quickly?

options.text: Exactly, in about 3 minutes
To within 1–2° in a few seconds
To within 6 seconds of arc in a few seconds
To within 1–2° in about 15 minutes

explanation: Coarse alignment gets the platform within 1–2° in a few seconds, which shortens the time needed for the fine stages.

question: How is fine levelling of an INS platform achieved?

options.text: By entering the aerodrome elevation
By aligning the platform with the airframe
By driving the accelerometer outputs to zero
By connecting the east gyro to the azimuth gimbal motor

explanation: A level horizontal accelerometer senses no component of gravity, so the platform is driven until both give zero output.

question: How long does fine levelling take, and to what accuracy?

options.text: About 1–1½ min, to about 6 seconds of arc
About 10 minutes, to within 1 minute of arc
About 3–4 minutes, to within 6 minutes of arc
A few seconds, to within 1–2°

explanation: Fine levelling takes up to about 1–1½ minutes and levels the platform to within about 6 seconds of arc.

question: In gyrocompassing, which gyro signal is used to align the platform with true north?

options.text: The vertical accelerometer
The north gyro, which senses earth rotation when aligned
The azimuth gyro, which senses magnetic north
The east gyro's earth-rate signal

explanation: With the platform correctly aligned, the east gyro's input axis senses no component of earth rotation. When misaligned it does, and its signal torques the azimuth gyro until the platform points to true north.

question: When the INS platform is correctly aligned in azimuth, what does the east gyro sense of the earth's rotation?

options.text: The full earth rate of 15°/h
No component of it
Earth rate × cos latitude
Earth rate × sin latitude

explanation: The east gyro's input axis lies east-west; the earth's rotation vector lies in the north-south vertical plane, so a correctly aligned east gyro senses none of it.

question: Which two conditions must be met before an INS is aligned?

options.text: Waypoints loaded, and the aircraft moving slowly
Accelerometers aligned with the airframe, and platform to magnetic north
Accelerometers levelled, and platform oriented to true north
Engines running, and the pitot heaters on

explanation: Alignment requires the accelerometers levelled (velocity set to zero) and the platform oriented to true north by gyrocompassing, with the position verified.

question: Why must the aircraft not be moved during INS alignment?

options.text: The battery cannot supply power while taxiing
The flux valve cannot be read on the move
Any motion is taken as an error and spoils the alignment
The waypoint memory is cleared when it moves

explanation: Alignment works by sensing only gravity and earth rotation. Any movement adds accelerations and rotations the system cannot separate, so alignment fails or is degraded.

question: Why does INS alignment take longer at high latitudes?

options.text: The accelerometers freeze in the cold air
The horizontal earth rate is weaker there
The gravity vector is not vertical there
The earth's magnetic field is weaker and steeper there

explanation: Gyrocompassing uses the horizontal component of earth rate, 15° per hour × cos latitude, which shrinks towards the poles. The signal is weaker, so alignment takes longer and near the poles may not be possible.

question: Schuler's imaginary earth pendulum has a length equal to:

options.text: The height of the aircraft above the surface
The circumference of the earth
One nautical mile
The radius of the earth

explanation: Schuler imagined a pendulum as long as the earth's radius, its bob at the earth's centre. Accelerating the suspension point would not disturb it, so a platform on it would stay level.

question: What is the period of the Schuler oscillation?

options.text: 84.4 minutes
60 minutes
24 hours
15.04 minutes

explanation: A pendulum the length of the earth's radius would oscillate with a period of 84.4 minutes. INS errors from a platform tilt oscillate with this period.

question: How is an INS platform kept normal to the local vertical as the aircraft moves over the earth?

options.text: By resetting the platform every 84.4 minutes
By using pendulous vanes, as in an air-driven attitude indicator
By feeding back velocity to torque the gyros
By a flux valve that senses the vertical field

explanation: The computed velocity is fed back to torque the levelling gyros so that the platform tilts at the rate the local vertical turns. This Schuler tuning keeps the accelerometers from sensing gravity.

question: Why does Schuler tuning keep INS errors "bounded" for a platform tilt?

options.text: The error reverses each time the aircraft turns through 180°
The error is removed by the pilot each hour
The error is cancelled by the radio updates
It oscillates with an 84.4-minute period

explanation: A small platform tilt produces an error that swings back and forth with the Schuler period rather than accumulating. Errors that grow with time are called unbounded.

question: What is an unbounded INS error?

options.text: One that grows with time, such as from a ground speed error
One that oscillates with the 84.4-minute Schuler period
One that appears only during manoeuvres
One that is limited to a few hundred metres

explanation: An unbounded error increases with time. A small ground speed error, integrated, gives a position error that keeps growing. Errors tied to the Schuler cycle are bounded.

question: What is the typical accuracy of an aircraft INS in navigation mode?

options.text: A position drift of about 1–2 NM per day
A position drift of about 1–2 NM per hour
No drift at all once aligned
A position drift of about 10 NM per minute

explanation: An INS drifts slowly, roughly 1–2 NM per hour of flight, because small gyro and accelerometer errors accumulate. Updating from a known fix removes the accumulated error.

question: Which rotation must the INS computer correct for, at about 15.04° per hour?

options.text: The earth's rotation
The Schuler oscillation
Transport wander towards the pole
The aircraft's rate of turn

explanation: The earth turns at about 15.04° per hour relative to the stars. The INS computer removes its effect so that the platform stays aligned to the local north and vertical.

question: On the INS control and display unit, what does the waypoint thumbwheel select?

options.text: The display of track and ground speed
The mode of the system: align, nav or attitude
The brightness of the displays
The waypoint to be loaded or checked

explanation: The waypoint selector is turned to the waypoint number when loading latitudes and longitudes before flight, reloading in flight or checking what is loaded.

question: What does the FROM/TO display on an INS control unit show?

options.text: The time to the next waypoint
The two waypoints of the leg being flown
The present position and the next fix
The departure and destination aerodromes of the flight

explanation: All read-outs and the flight director and autopilot commands are based on the leg between the FROM and TO waypoints, so a wrong pair or a wrongly loaded position leads the aircraft off course.

question: What is the track change push-button of an INS used for?

options.text: To dim the displays
To change the displayed track from true to magnetic
To set the two waypoints to fly between
To update the present position over a fix

explanation: The track change button sets a new FROM/TO pair, for example to go direct to a waypoint or when the system is not flying the waypoints in sequence.

question: In AUTO mode, when does the INS ALERT light come on and go out?

options.text: Steady at 2 minutes to go; out at the track change
On steady 30 seconds before the waypoint, out 2 minutes after it
Flashing 2 minutes before the waypoint, out overhead
On steady overhead the waypoint, out 2 minutes later

explanation: In AUTO the alert light comes on steady about 2 minutes to run and goes out as the system changes track overhead the waypoint.

question: In MANUAL mode, how does the INS ALERT light behave approaching a waypoint?

options.text: Steady at 30 seconds to go, until the track changes
Flashing at 2 minutes to go, then steady from 30 seconds to go
Off until the waypoint, then flashing for 30 seconds
Steady at 2 min; flashing from 30 s until changed

explanation: In MANUAL the light comes on steady 2 minutes before the waypoint, starts to flash 30 seconds before it, and keeps flashing until the crew changes the track.

question: Why does the INS ALERT annunciator not come on at low speed?

options.text: It needs the air data computer, which is off on the ground
It is inhibited below a set speed, such as 100 kt
It is inhibited until the first waypoint is passed
It works only above the transition altitude

explanation: The alert annunciator does not illuminate below a set ground speed, typically either 100 kt or 250 kt depending on the system, so it does not trigger while taxiing.

question: What does the BAT annunciator on an INS control unit indicate?

options.text: Alignment is complete and the system is ready
The battery needs to be replaced
It is running on its internal battery
The waypoint memory is full

explanation: The battery annunciator shows that the INS has lost its normal supply and is running on internal or standby battery power.

question: With the INS mode switch in AUTO, what happens as each waypoint is overflown?

options.text: The INS changes to the next track automatically
The crew must change the FROM/TO waypoints by hand
The INS enters attitude mode
The ALERT light starts to flash until reset

explanation: In AUTO the system switches from one track to the next as each waypoint is passed. In MANUAL the operator must update the FROM/TO read-out at each waypoint.

question: In general terms, what does the REMOTE position of the INS auto/manual/remote switch allow?

options.text: Use of the INS with the main power off
Navigation using radio updates only
Loading several INSs from one control unit
Control of the INS from the ground

explanation: Its exact function depends on the system, but in general REMOTE allows waypoints to be inserted into several INSs at the same time from one control and display unit.

question: What is the HOLD push-button on an INS control unit mainly used for?

options.text: Holding the present waypoint so it is not passed
Updating the INS position when over a reliable fix
Freezing the alignment while the aircraft is towed
Holding the aircraft in a racetrack pattern

explanation: HOLD is pressed as a reliable fix, such as a VOR overhead, is passed. The displayed position is frozen so it can be compared with the fix and the position updated.

question: What is the INSERT push-button on an INS control unit used for?

options.text: Inserting the INS into the autopilot loop
Changing from the FROM to the TO waypoint
Inserting a holding pattern at a waypoint
Entering keyboard data into the system

explanation: The keyboard is used to type data such as waypoint coordinates or the present position, and INSERT enters that data into the system.

question: Which INS display shows the drift angle?

options.text: Heading and drift angle, HDG/DA
Cross-track error and track angle error, XTK/TKE
Distance and time, DIS/TIME
Track and ground speed, TK/GS

explanation: HDG/DA displays true heading and drift angle. TK/GS shows track and ground speed, and XTK/TKE the cross-track distance and track angle error.

question: A pilot wants to check that two sequential waypoints are correctly entered. Which comparison is useful?

options.text: The INS wind against the forecast wind
The INS heading against the standby compass
The leg distance against the flight plan
The INS ground speed against the indicated airspeed

explanation: The DIS/TIME display gives the distance between the selected waypoints, which should match the flight plan; the desired track for the leg can also be checked against the plan.

question: What does the INS track angle error (TKE) show?

options.text: The distance off the desired track
The error in the initial alignment heading
The angle between heading and track
The angle between track and desired track

explanation: Track angle error is the angular difference between the track being made good and the desired track. The distance off track is the cross-track error, XTK; the angle between heading and track is drift.
